body:
Surat's location and commercial importance

Surat developed on the banks of the Tapi river in western Gujarat. Its access to maritime routes made it one of the most important ports of the Mughal period.

Surat was an emporium of western trade. Goods from several production centres were brought to the city, purchased by merchants and carried to overseas markets. Its commercial importance depended both on access to shipping and on connections with the inland economy.

The gateway to West Asia

Surat was a major gateway for trade with West Asia through the Gulf of Hormuz. Gujarati merchants also maintained commercial connections with ports around the Red Sea, Persian Gulf and East Africa.

Textiles and spices were important goods in these trading networks. Overseas exchange also brought precious metals and commodities from other regions into Indian markets.

The Gate to Mecca

Surat was known as the Gate to Mecca because ships carrying Muslim pilgrims departed from the port on journeys towards the holy city of Mecca.

This description refers to Surat's role in pilgrimage transport. Its importance as a trading port and its importance as a pilgrimage gateway were connected through maritime routes, but they were distinct functions.

European trading companies at Surat

During the 17th century, Portuguese, Dutch and English traders maintained commercial establishments at Surat. The English East India Company obtained permission to establish a factory at Surat in 1613.

Factory in the historical trading context

A factory was a commercial establishment where a European trading company's representatives conducted business, maintained accounts and stored goods. It was not necessarily a mechanised manufacturing plant.

The English, Dutch and Portuguese were not the only people involved in Surat's commerce. The city also contained Indian merchant communities and traders connected with West Asian and other overseas commercial networks.

The European companies sought access to existing markets. Their representatives purchased goods from Indian merchants and arranged their storage and shipment. They therefore depended on the commercial organisation already present in Gujarat.

A diverse urban society

Surat's prosperity attracted merchants, artisans, sailors, transport workers and visitors from different regions and religious communities. Markets, warehouses, lodging facilities and financial services supported its trade.

Commercial activity also connected the port with the Mughal political establishment. The empire benefited from a prosperous trading city through revenue and the resources associated with maritime commerce.

Prelims focus

  • Surat was situated on the Tapi river in western Gujarat.
  • It was a major Mughal-period emporium of western trade.
  • The Gulf of Hormuz connected Surat's trade with West Asia.
  • Surat was called the Gate to Mecca because pilgrim ships departed from the port.
  • The English East India Company established a factory at Surat in 1613.
  • Trap: A 17th-century trading factory was not necessarily an industrial manufacturing unit.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, 2020–21 printing, Towns, Traders and Craftspersons, pp. 84–85; Gujarat Government, NRI Division, History of Surat, section on Mughal-era commerce and pilgrimage, consulted 19 November 2026; Governing Over Distance: Delegating Trust and Dealing with Disorder in the Early East India Company Trade, The Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History, 2024, discussion of the Surat factory established in 1613, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Surat: The Mughal Empire's Western Maritime Gateway

body:
The people who supported commercial prosperity

The commercial economy of Mughal Gujarat involved more than rulers and port officials. Cultivators supplied agricultural products; artisans manufactured goods; merchants organised purchases and sales; transport workers moved merchandise; and bankers facilitated payments.

These groups were closely connected. A merchant exporting cloth from Surat, for example, depended on cotton producers, spinners, weavers, dyers, carriers and financial intermediaries.

Gujarati merchant communities

Gujarati traders included Hindu Baniyas and Muslim Bohras, both of whom participated in extensive trading networks. Their commercial connections reached the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, East Africa, Southeast Asia and China.

These networks carried textiles, spices and other goods to foreign markets and brought commodities from other regions into Gujarat.

Surat also had wealthy merchants and financiers. Virji Vora was a prominent merchant associated with the city's Mughal-period commerce.

Textile production and specialised labour

Cotton textiles were among Gujarat's most important commercial products. Different workers contributed to different stages of production:

  • Cultivators: Grew cotton and crops such as indigo.
  • Spinners: Converted cotton fibre into yarn.
  • Weavers: Produced cloth using yarn.
  • Dyers and printers: Coloured and decorated yarn or finished fabric.
  • Merchants: Purchased, financed, transported and sold the finished goods.

Women participated in agricultural and artisanal production, including spinning and other labour associated with household and commercial manufacture. Commercial prosperity therefore depended on work performed in both towns and villages.

Surat's zari textiles

Surat's textiles were especially known for decorative gold lace borders, called zari. Such fabrics were sold in markets extending to West Asia, Africa and Europe.

Demand for textiles supported skilled craft production, but commercial wealth was not distributed equally among all participants. Wealthy merchants and major officials could control substantial resources, while cultivators and artisans remained dependent on work, markets and credit.

Bankers, mahajans and hundis

Large-scale trade required methods of transferring money between distant places. Merchant-bankers and moneychangers helped meet this need.

Surat's Kathiawad seths and mahajans operated important banking houses. One financial instrument used in commercial networks was the hundi.

Hundi

A hundi was a written financial instrument that could record a deposit or support payment at another place through a recognised commercial network. It enabled merchants to transfer financial claims without necessarily carrying the equivalent amount of cash throughout a journey.

The commercial acceptance of Surat hundis extended to distant markets such as Cairo, Basra and Antwerp. This illustrates the geographic reach of Surat's banking and trading connections.

A hundi should be distinguished from a coin. It depended on the credibility and arrangements of the merchants or bankers involved, rather than being an ordinary piece of metallic currency.

Trade, revenue and the imperial household

Surat's commercial importance also benefited members of the Mughal ruling establishment. Jahanara, a daughter of Emperor Shah Jahan, received revenues associated with the port city of Surat.

This connection demonstrates how the income of a trading centre could support imperial elites as well as merchants.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarati merchant groups included Hindu Baniyas and Muslim Bohras.
  • Surat was known for textiles with gold lace borders called zari.
  • Hundi was a financial instrument used in merchant and banking networks.
  • Surat hundis were recognised in markets including Cairo, Basra and Antwerp.
  • Virji Vora was a prominent Surat merchant.
  • Jahanara, the daughter of Shah Jahan, received revenues associated with Surat.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, 2020–21 printing, Towns, Traders and Craftspersons, pp. 79–80 and 84–85; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Peasants, Zamindars and the State, pp. 206 and 215–216, and Kings and Chronicles, p. 243; IGNOU, MHI-10, Unit 30, Cities in the 18th Century-1, section 30.4, Ahmadabad, pp. 59–60, consulted 19 November 2026; Gujarat Government, NRI Division, History of Surat, section on Mughal-era merchants, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The connected roles of agricultural producers, textile workers, merchants, ports and banking networks.

title: Merchants, Craftspeople, Banking and Gujarat's Social Economy

body:
Why Surat became a target

During the reign of Mughal emperor Aurangzeb (1658–1707), the Maratha leader Shivaji challenged Mughal authority in western India and the Deccan.

Surat was a particularly important target because it combined concentrated commercial wealth with political value to the Mughal Empire. Its merchants handled valuable goods and money, and its prosperity supported imperial interests.

The 2 major raids on Surat

Shivaji carried out major raids on Surat in:

  • January 1664: The first major raid disrupted the wealthy trading city and caused substantial losses.
  • October 1670: Shivaji raided Surat again, demonstrating the continuing challenge to Mughal authority and commercial security.

These were attacks on a major Mughal commercial centre. They should not be confused with the later establishment of lasting Maratha political authority over territories in Gujarat.

A raid is not the same as annexation. Shivaji's attacks on Surat in 1664 and 1670 did not themselves establish permanent Maratha government over the port city.

Effects on commerce and administration

The raids exposed the difficulties Mughal authorities faced in protecting an important trading centre. Merchants risked losing goods and money, while insecurity could interrupt transport, commercial transactions and revenue collection.

The consequences extended beyond individual raids. Mughal political difficulties, competition among European maritime powers and the increasing importance of Bombay gradually changed the balance of western Indian commerce.

Surat and the rise of Bombay

Bombay, now Mumbai, became an increasingly important English commercial centre. It was transferred to the English East India Company in 1668. In 1687, Bombay replaced Surat as the company's headquarters for its western Indian trade.

This change helped strengthen Bombay's commercial position. Surat's relative importance declined towards the end of the 17th century and during the 18th century.

However, Surat did not immediately cease trading. Its established merchant, financial and manufacturing connections continued to support commercial activity. The decline was a change in its relative position, not the sudden disappearance of the city's economy.

Prelims focus

  • Aurangzeb ruled from 1658 to 1707.
  • Shivaji's first major raid on Surat occurred in 1664.
  • Shivaji raided Surat again in 1670.
  • Bombay was transferred to the English East India Company in 1668.
  • Bombay became the company's western Indian headquarters in 1687.
  • Trap: The Surat raids did not themselves amount to permanent Maratha annexation of the city.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, 2020–21 printing, The Mughal Empire, pp. 49 and 56, and Towns, Traders and Craftspersons, pp. 84–85; B. G. Gokhale, Surat in the Seventeenth Century, 1979, discussion of Shivaji's 1664 raid and its commercial effects; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Volume I, Part I, History of Gujarat, section on Mughal Gujarat and the Surat raids of 1664 and 1670, consulted 19 November 2026; Om Prakash, study of the English East India Company's trade in India, London School of Economics, discussion of Surat and Bombay, p. 8, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Shivaji's Raids on Surat and the Challenge to Mughal Authority

body:
The weakening of Mughal provincial authority

Emperor Aurangzeb died in 1707. During the following decades, Mughal central authority weakened, and provincial governors, powerful nobles and local chiefs increasingly pursued their own interests.

In Gujarat, disputes over provincial office and revenue created opportunities for other regional powers. The decline of effective control from Delhi did not mean that the Mughal provincial administration disappeared everywhere at once. Political authority changed through a series of local contests, alliances and conquests.

Rajput governors and provincial competition

Rajput rulers who had served the Mughal Empire also sought control over influential provincial offices. Ajit Singh of Jodhpur held the governorship of Gujarat, while Sawai Jai Singh of Amber held the governorship of Malwa. These appointments were renewed in 1713.

The distinction between the 2 governors and their provinces is important because their names and offices can easily be confused.

The Marathas enter Gujarat's political struggles

The Maratha state had developed through resistance to Mughal authority under Shivaji. In the 18th century, effective leadership of the wider Maratha state came increasingly into the hands of the Peshwas, or principal ministers, whose political centre was Poona (Pune).

Maratha power expanded into Gujarat during the 1720s. Military intervention, alliances and revenue claims gradually weakened the position of Mughal officers and other regional authorities.

The Marathas did not gain complete and uniform control over the whole province in a single campaign. Different territories came under changing arrangements involving the Peshwa, Maratha chiefs and local rulers.

The Gaekwads of Baroda

The Gaekwad family became an important Maratha ruling house in Gujarat. Its rise was closely connected with the growth of Maratha power in southern Gujarat.

Pilaji Rao Gaekwad captured Songadh in 1726. His successor Damaji Rao Gaekwad captured Baroda in 1734. Baroda, now Vadodara, became an important centre of Gaekwad power.

Another decisive development occurred in 1753, when combined forces associated with the Peshwa and Gaekwad captured Ahmedabad. This marked a major stage in the displacement of Mughal provincial authority in Gujarat.

Chauth and sardeshmukhi

Maratha expansion involved claims to revenue as well as territorial control. Two important terms were chauth and sardeshmukhi.

Revenue claimMeaningRate
ChauthA Maratha claim to a share of assessed land revenue, often associated with political or military authority.25%
SardeshmukhiAn additional revenue claim associated with the position of the chief revenue collector.About 10%

These were Maratha revenue claims, not names for the Mughal zabt system. Their collection depended on the political arrangements and authority established in particular territories. It would be incorrect to assume that every locality paid both levies continuously or under identical conditions.

Effects on Ahmedabad and regional trade

Political struggles in Gujarat affected the economy. During periods of instability, merchants could face additional financial demands, while insecurity interfered with production and trade.

In the second quarter of the 18th century, some weavers migrated from Ahmedabad to Surat and other places as political and commercial conditions worsened.

However, the economic consequences were not uniformly negative or permanent. After Maratha authority became more secure in Ahmedabad during the 1750s, efforts to restore peace and commercial activity helped encourage artisans and merchants to return. Textile production and trade revived.

This history illustrates a central relationship: political instability could disrupt commerce, while greater security could help production and markets recover. The weakening of Mughal authority therefore produced both conflict and new regional political arrangements.

Key political and commercial developments

Year or periodDevelopment
1707Death of Aurangzeb; Mughal central authority weakened during the following decades.
1713Ajit Singh's Gujarat governorship and Sawai Jai Singh's Malwa governorship were renewed.
1720sMaratha expansion and revenue claims increased in Gujarat.
1726Pilaji Rao Gaekwad captured Songadh.
1734Damaji Rao Gaekwad captured Baroda.
1753Combined Peshwa–Gaekwad forces captured Ahmedabad.

Prelims focus

  • Aurangzeb died in 1707.
  • Ajit Singh of Jodhpur governed Gujarat; Sawai Jai Singh of Amber governed Malwa.
  • The Peshwa was the Maratha principal minister; Poona was the Maratha political centre.
  • Pilaji Rao Gaekwad captured Songadh in 1726; Damaji Rao Gaekwad captured Baroda in 1734.
  • Peshwa–Gaekwad forces captured Ahmedabad in 1753.
  • Chauth was 25%; sardeshmukhi was approximately 10%.
  • Trap: Maratha political expansion did not bring every part of Gujarat under a single, uniform arrangement at the same time.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, 2020–21 printing, Eighteenth-Century Political Formations, pp. 138–151; IGNOU, MHI-10, Unit 30, Cities in the 18th Century-1, section 30.4, Ahmadabad, pp. 59–60, consulted 19 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Vadodara District Administration, History, section on the Gaekwads, updated 9 July 2025 and consulted 19 November 2026; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Volume I, Part I, History of Gujarat, account of the capture of Ahmedabad in 1753, consulted 19 November 2026.]
